Compounds via Intermolecular Boryl Group Transfer†

Comprehensive Summary  
 
Allenylboronates are valuable synthetic building blocks and have garnered significant interest. However, their 1,3-diboyl substituted 
analogs have not been reported. Herein, we disclosed a novel method for creating  1,3-diboyl allenes from gem-iododiboron com-
pounds and alkynyl Grignard reagents . The starting materials are initially converted into the corresponding propargylic  
gem-bis(boronates), which then undergo an intermolecular boryl group transfer  to afford 1,3-diboyl allenes, as confirmed by mech a-
nistic studies. This method features good tolerance to steric hindrance and is compatible with a wide variety of functional groups.

Background and Originality Content 
Allenes are a unique class of unsaturated compounds with a 
cumulative double-bond skeleton, having widespread applications 
in natural product synthesis, pharmaceutical chemistry, and mate-
rials science. [1] Allenylboron compounds, [2] in particular, have 
proven themselves to be valuable building blocks in propargyla-
tion, allenylation,[3-4] and many other useful transformations.[5] 
Moreover, the versatile C —B bond can be readily converted into 
various functional grou ps.[6] Thus, chemists have persisted in 
seeking methods for the facile synthesis of allenylboronates from 
readily available starting materials. Currently, the two major ap-
proaches are: 1) boryl substitution of propargylic compounds 
bearing a leaving group [7] and 2) hydroboration of enynes  with 
HB(pin) or HB(cat) [8] (Scheme 1A). Recently, more strategies, such 
as olefin metathesis[9] and hydrazination/fragmentation of alkynyl 
boronates,[10] have been reported . Intriguingly, allenylboronates 
can also be accesse d from the isomerization of propargylic boron 
compounds,[11-12] featuring an intramolecular boryl group migra -
tion as the key step (Scheme 1B).  Despite the extensive study of 
the synthesis and application of allenylboronates , research on 
diboryl-substituted allenes remains elusive. Given the unique 
reactivities of the analogous diboryl alkene  species,[13] the syn -
thetic protocols for diboryl allenes are highly desired. 
Halogenated geminal bis(boronates) have recently emerged as 
versatile synthons and attracted significant attention.[14] Inde-
pendent research by Cho,[15] Liu,[16] and Hong[17] groups has led to 
the development of substitution reactions of halogenated gem-di-
boron compounds with various nucleophiles. While most sp3- and 
sp2-hybridized Grignard reagents were compatible and yielded 
formal substitution products,[17] we discovered that the sp-hybrid-
ized Grignard reagents, i.e., alkynyl magnesium halides, produced 
1,3-diboryl allenes predominantly (Scheme 1C). In this paper, we 
present the development of this method and the mechanistic 
studies behind this unprecedented transformation. 
Scheme 1  Synthesis of allenylboronates and 1,3-diboryl allenes  
 
Results and Discussion 
Our investigation commenced with the addition of alkynyl 
Grignard reagent 2a to an α-halogenated gem-diboron compound 
1 (Table 1). According to our previous studies, [17] the halogen 
substituent and the cosolvent were found crucial to the reaction. 
After initial test s, excellent yield was observed when the 
gem-diboryl iodide 1c was employed as the substrate (e ntries 
1—3). Due to the lower reactivity of the sp-hybridized carbanion, 
magnesium-iodine exchange, which was previously observed with 
aryl and alkyl Grignard reagents, did not occur . To our delight, the 
propargyl gem-diboron product 3a was not generated, which is 
otherwise challenging to separate. The addition of toluene as th e 
cosolvent was not necessary  compared to pure THF or diethyl 
ether/THF system (entries 4 and 5). However, with toluene, the 
reaction was homogeneous, which was preferred for further 
study. 1,4-Dioxane, DME , and cyclohexane, however, hampered 
the reaction efficiency and provided 3a as the major product 
(entries 6 —8). Lastly, alkynyl lithium and zinc reagents were 
investigated, and the desired product was also observed, albeit in 
lower yield (entries 9 and 10).

With the optimal condition in hand, the scope of Grignard r e-
agents was explored first using 1c as the standard substrate (Table 
2A). The diboryl alle ne skeleton of 4a was confirmed by single 
crystal X -ray diffraction. A gram -scale experiment was also pe r-
formed under the standard conditions. The yield slightly dimin-
ished due to the prolonged purific ation on silica gel. This protocol 
was not sensitive to the steric hindrance on the far side of the 
alkynyl reagents. Products with both linear  chains and hindered 
quaternary carbon centers were obtained in good yields (4b—4e). 
Grignard reagents bearing alkenyl (4g) and aryl groups ( 4h—4p) 
also performed well. A variety of  electron-donating and wit h-
drawing substituents at the ortho-, meta- and para-positions were 
compatible with little impact on the overall efficiency . Notably, 
this method was also competent to naphthyl group (4o) and aro-
matic heterocycles (4f and 4p). Additionally, a correspond ing 
product with geminal silyl and boryl substitution (4q) was o b-
tained in excellent yield, providing potential for chemoselective 
transformation.[7a,18]  
Next, we examined the scope of the iododiboron compounds 
using a 3 -phenyl-1-propyne-derived Grignard reagent (Table 2B). 
A wide range of linear and branched alkyl substituents with di f-
ferent sizes and functional groups were surveyed. T he products 
were obtained in high yields in most cases  (4r—4ag). Notably, the 
sterically hindered tert-butyl group  was well tolerated ( 4y). De-
spite the use of gem-diboryl bromide due to the preparation 
method of the starting material,[19] high efficiency was maintained. 
Functional groups such as bromo and pyridyl groups, acetal, ether, 
and allyl groups  were all compatible. However, the product pos-
sessing an ester group  was collected in o nly 45% yield ( 4af). This 
inferior result was presumab ly attributed to the coordination b e-
tween the carbonyl oxygen and the boron atom, which might

Our efforts were then devoted to elucidating the reaction 
mechanism. Initially, substrate 5, in which one of the B(pin) 
groups was replaced with a methyl group, was subjected to the 
standard condition (Scheme 2A). The reaction efficiency de -
creased significantly, and more importantly, propargyl boronate 6 
emerged as the primary product. This out come aligned with the 
results in Table 1 ( entries 6—8), suggesting that the reaction may 
involve a formal substitution followed by an isomerization step, 
both potentially promoted by the geminal diboryl groups. To fur -
ther validate this hypothesis, we carr ied out the reaction using 
iododiboron 1c at –30 °C, and isolated the corresponding propar-
gyl gem-diboron compound 8 as the sole product in 52% yield 
(Scheme 2B). Subsequently, with the addition of a catalytic 
amount of Grignard reagent, compound 8 underwent complete 
isomerization to 1,3 -diboryl allene 4b in 80% NMR yield (Scheme 
2C).  
In previous studies by Soderquist and Zhu (Scheme 1B), in -
tramolecular boryl migration was proposed to explain the isomer -
ization.[11] To investigate whether our react ion follows a similar 
mechanism, we conducted an isotope -labeling crossover experi -
ment (Scheme 2D). We initially combined 10B-labeled 1c[20] with 
unlabeled 1d in a 1  : 1 ratio and then exposed the mixture to the 
standard condition. The resulting products, 4b and 4ae, were 
isolated and analyzed using high -resolution mass spectroscopy 
(HRMS). Upon comparing the spectra of the collected product 4b 
to that of authentic 10B-4b and unlabeled 4b with natural abun -
dance, it became evident that there was a scrambling of boryl 
groups between 10B-1c and 1d. The same phenomenon was also 
observed for 4ae (for HRMS spectra, see Supporting Information). 
This outcome strongly indicated that an intermolecular pathway is 
the predominant, if not the sole, route during the isomerization. 
To provide additional mechanistic insight s, we performed an-
other isotope-labeling experiment. Specifically, we conducted the 
isomerization of 10B-8 in the presence of a stoichiometric amount 
of unlabeled alkynyl boronate 9 (Scheme 2E). The HRMS spectrum 
of product mixB-4b further confirmed the involvement of an al -
kynyl boronate species in the major pathway.

Scheme 2  Mechanistic studies 
 
 
In light of the mechanistic experiments and our previous 
studies,[17] a plausible mechanism is proposed in Scheme 2F. Sub-
strate 10 was initially converted into gem-diboryl alkyne 12 
through the formation of ate -complex 11, followed by a 
1,2-metallate shift. The coordination of compound 12 with excess 
Grignard reagent generates ate -complex 13, and the cleavage of 
the C —B bond leads to the formation of a more stable 
sp2-hybridized carbanion 14. This carbanion can serve as a Lewis 
base to abstract a boryl group from alkynyl boronate 9 to afford 
the desired product 16. The resulting alkynyl carbanion 15 can 
then activate another molecule of 12 in a catalytic manner (Path A 
with red arrows). The alternative pathway involves a boryl transfer 
from another molecule of 12 through the intermediacy of 
ate-complex 17, yield ing compounds 16 and 14, which can then 
sustain a chain proc ess (Path B with blue arrows) . Based on the 
current information, the occurrence of Path A can be confirmed. 
However, both pathways appear to contribute to the reaction, and 
it remains unclear which of them is predominant.

Conclusions 
In summary, we have disclosed the first example of accessing 
1,3-diboryl allenes from gem-iododiboron compounds  in the 
presence of alkynyl Grignard reagents . The reaction is highly effi -
cient and can accommodate steric hindrance and various func -
tional gro ups. Mechanistic studies have suggested that the cas -
cade process consists of a formal substitution and a subsequent 
isomerization. The isotope -labeling crossover experiment indi -
cated that the isomerization proceeds through an unconventional 
intermolecular boryl group transfer . Utilization of the products 
was also briefly demonstrated. 
Experimental 
In an argon -filled glove box, to a 15 mL vial equipped with a 
magnetic stir bar was added the iododiboron compound (0.1 
mmol, 1.0 equiv.). The vial was sealed with a polypropylene 
open-top cap with PTFE/silicone septum, then removed from the 
glove box. Toluene (1.0 mL) was added and the vial was cooled in 
an ice-cold water bath. Grignard reagent (0.11 mmol, 1.1 equiv.) 
was slowly added. The mixture was then warm ed to room tem -
perature and stirred for 3 h. Upon completion, the reaction was 
quenched with sat. NH 4Cl solution (2 mL) and extracted with Et 2O 
(3 x 2 mL). The combined organic layers were dried over Na 2SO4, 
filtered, and concentrated in vacuo , and the crude reaction mix -
ture was purified by column chromatography on pre-dried silica 
gel.

Comprehensive Summary

Allenylboronates are valuable synthetic building blocks and have garnered significant interest. However, their 1,3-diboyl substituted
analogs have not been reported. Herein, we disclosed a novel method for creating 1,3-diboyl allenes from gem-iododiboron com-
pounds and alkynyl Grignard reagents. The starting materials are initially converted into the corresponding propargylic
gem-bis(boronates), which then undergo an intermolecular boryl group transfer to afford 1,3-diboyl allenes, as confirmed by mecha-
nistic studies. This method features good tolerance to steric hindrance and is compatible with a wide variety of functional groups.

Our investigation commenced with the addition of alkynyl

substituent and the cosolvent were found crucial to the reaction.
After initial tests, excellent yield was observed when the
gem-diboryl iodide 1c was employed as the substrate (entries
1—3). Due to the lower reactivity of the sp-hybridized carbanion,
magnesium-iodine exchange, which was previously observed with

Conclusions

In summary, we have disclosed the first example of accessing
1,3-diboryl allenes from gem-iododiboron compounds in the
presence of alkynyl Grignard reagents. The reaction is highly effi-
cient and can accommodate steric hindrance and various func-
tional groups. Mechanistic studies have suggested that the cas-
cade process consists of a formal substitution and a subsequent
isomerization. The isotope-labeling crossover experiment indi-
cated that the isomerization proceeds through an unconventional
intermolecular boryl group transfer. Utilization of the products
was also briefly demonstrated.
Experimental

In an argon-filled glove box, to a 15 mL vial equipped with a
magnetic stir bar was added the iododiboron compound (0.1
mmol, 1.0 equiv.). The vial was sealed with a polypropylene
open-top cap with PTFE/silicone septum, then removed from the
glove box. Toluene (1.0 mL) was added and the vial was cooled in
an ice-cold water bath. Grignard reagent (0.11 mmol, 1.1 equiv.)
was slowly added. The mixture was then warmed to room tem-
perature and stirred for 3 h. Upon completion, the reaction was
quenched with sat.
\mathsf { N H } _ { 4 } \mathsf { C l }
solution (2 mL) and extracted with Et O
(3 x 2 mL). The combined organic layers were dried over Na<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>,
filtered, and concentrated in vacuo, and the crude reaction mix-
ture was purified by column chromatography on pre-dried silica
gel.
